s.u1.title: Two laws nobody can break
s.u1.blurb: Mass does not appear or vanish, and a compound will not take more of one element than it wants.
s.u2.title: What one atom is
s.u2.blurb: The dot from the first chapter finally gets a name, a symbol and a mass.
s.u3.title: Atoms that travel together
s.u3.blurb: Most atoms are not found alone. What they form, and what to call it.
s.u4.title: Writing the formula
s.u4.blurb: Why magnesium chloride is MgCl2 and never MgCl.
s.u5.title: Adding up the mass
s.u5.blurb: Once you know the formula, the mass is arithmetic.
ch3.u1.definition: Burn a candle and it seems to disappear. Rust a nail and it seems to gain. Weigh everything, including the gases, and the total never changes. Mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction: that is the law of conservation of mass, and it is why a chemical equation has to balance.
a.ch3-u1-read-1.title: Nothing is lost, nothing is gained
ch3.u1.flask.predict.prompt: Two solutions react and give off a gas. You weigh the flask before and after. What happens to the reading?
ch3.u1.flask.predict.o3: It depends on whether the flask is sealed
ch3.u1.flask.observe: One of them changed and one did not. What was different?
ch3.u1.flask.explain: Mass was conserved both times. In the open flask the carbon dioxide simply left before you weighed it, which looks like loss and is not.
ask.ch3-u1-sealedflask-2.opensystem.q: So the open flask broke the law?
ask.ch3-u1-sealedflask-2.opensystem.a:
No, and this is the distinction worth holding on to. The law is about everything that took part, not about what happens to still be in your flask. The carbon dioxide did not stop existing; it went into the room. Put a balloon over the neck and catch it, and the reading goes back to being unchanged.

This is why chemists talk about a closed system. Not because mass behaves differently in a sealed container, but because a sealed container is the only place you can check.
a.ch3-u1-sealedflask-2.title: Weigh it, mix it, weigh it again
a.ch3-u1-sealedflask-2.blurb: The same reaction in a sealed flask and an open one. Weigh before and after each time.
ch3.u1.ratio.predict.prompt: You have plenty of both elements. Can you make a compound with any ratio of the two you choose?
ch3.u1.ratio.predict.o0: Yes, you just get different amounts
ch3.u1.ratio.predict.o2: No, only one ratio combines completely
ch3.u1.ratio.observe: Which ratios left something sitting in the dish?
ch3.u1.ratio.explain: A compound takes its elements in one fixed ratio by mass and refuses the rest. That is the law of constant proportions, and it is why water from a tap, a river or a laboratory is the same substance.
ch3.u1.ratio.closing: Three grams of carbon with eight grams of oxygen, every time. Double both and it still works. Add oxygen without adding carbon and the extra just sits there. This is the same 3 to 8 the questions after this one ask about.
ask.ch3-u1-ratiomixer-3.whyfixed.q: Why should the ratio be fixed? Who decides it?
ask.ch3-u1-ratiomixer-3.whyfixed.a:
Nothing decides it. It falls out of the fact that atoms combine in whole numbers.

One carbon atom takes exactly two oxygen atoms, so carbon dioxide is that one pairing repeated as many times as you like. A carbon atom weighs 12 u and the two oxygens 32 u between them, and that is where 3 to 8 comes from. The mass ratio is just the atom ratio weighed, and you cannot have half an atom left over waiting for a partner.
a.ch3-u1-ratiomixer-3.title: The ratio that will not budge
a.ch3-u1-ratiomixer-3.blurb: Put in as much of each as you like. See how much is left over.
ch3.u1.calc.c0.prompt: A 0.24 g sample of a compound of boron and oxygen contains 0.096 g of boron. What percentage of the compound is boron, by weight?
ch3.u1.calc.c0.s0: Divide the boron by the total
ch3.u1.calc.c0.trap: Dividing by the oxygen instead of by the whole sample. The percentage is of the compound, not of the other element.
ch3.u1.calc.c1.prompt: The same 0.24 g sample contains 0.144 g of oxygen. What percentage is oxygen?
ch3.u1.calc.c1.s0: Divide the oxygen by the total
ch3.u1.calc.c1.trap: Forgetting to check: the two percentages have to add to 100, and they do.
a.ch3-u1-calc-4.title: Percentage composition
ch3.u1.quiz.q0.prompt: 3.0 g of carbon burnt in 8.00 g of oxygen gives 11.00 g of carbon dioxide. Burn 3.00 g of carbon in 50.00 g of oxygen instead. How much carbon dioxide forms?
ch3.u1.quiz.q0.f0: That adds up everything you put in. The extra oxygen did not react: carbon takes 8 g and no more.
ch3.u1.quiz.q0.f1: Right. The ratio is fixed, so 3 g of carbon takes 8 g of oxygen and leaves 42 g of oxygen unreacted.
ch3.u1.quiz.q0.o2: Impossible to say without more information
ch3.u1.quiz.q0.f2: You have enough. The first sentence tells you the ratio, and the ratio does not change.
ch3.u1.quiz.q0.f3: The amount is fixed, not somewhere in a range. Extra oxygen simply sits there.
ch3.u1.quiz.q1.f0: Mass is conserved here too, but it is not what fixes the answer.
ch3.u1.quiz.q1.f1: Right. The fixed ratio is what stops the extra oxygen joining in.
ch3.u1.quiz.q1.f2: Conservation of mass holds, but it would allow 53 g. Only the fixed ratio rules that out.
ch3.u1.quiz.q1.f3: One of them does the work here.
a.ch3-u1-quiz-5.title: Which law governs it?
ch3.u2.definition: Both laws make sense at once if matter is made of atoms: particles that cannot be broken down by a chemical reaction, that have a fixed mass for each element, and that combine in small whole numbers. Mass is conserved because the atoms are only rearranged. The ratio is fixed because you cannot use half an atom.
a.ch3-u2-read-1.title: Dalton's answer
ch3.u2.sort.i0.label: Hydrogen, H
ch3.u2.sort.i0.why: The first letter, and nothing else to remember.
ch3.u2.sort.i1.label: Carbon, C
ch3.u2.sort.i2.label: Calcium, Ca
ch3.u2.sort.i2.why: First two letters, because C was already taken by carbon.
ch3.u2.sort.i3.label: Sodium, Na
ch3.u2.sort.i3.why: From natrium. Nothing in the English word gives you an N.
ch3.u2.sort.i4.label: Potassium, K
ch3.u2.sort.i5.label: Iron, Fe
ch3.u2.sort.i6.label: Copper, Cu
ch3.u2.sort.i7.label: Silver, Ag
ask.ch3-u2-sort-2.whylatin.q: Why keep the old names? It would be simpler if sodium were S.
ask.ch3-u2-sort-2.whylatin.a:
S was already sulphur, and the symbols were agreed before English became the language chemistry is published in. Berzelius chose them from Latin in 1813 precisely so that chemists writing in Swedish, German, French and English would all write the same thing.

That is still true, and it is the reason symbols are not translated anywhere in this app: Fe is Fe in every language on Earth, which is a small piece of international agreement that has held for two centuries.
a.ch3-u2-sort-2.title: Name to symbol
a.ch3-u2-sort-2.blurb: Some symbols are the first letter of the English name. Others come from Latin, and those are the ones that catch people out.
ch3.u2.calc.c0.prompt: Atomic masses are given relative to one twelfth of a carbon-12 atom. If carbon is 12 u, and one oxygen atom is 16 u, how many times heavier than carbon is oxygen?
ch3.u2.calc.c0.s0: Divide the oxygen mass by the carbon mass
ch3.u2.calc.c0.trap: Treating u as grams. It is a ratio, not a weight you could put on a balance.
ch3.u2.calc.c1.prompt: A compound contains one calcium atom (40 u) and two chlorine atoms (35.5 u each). What is the total in u?
ch3.u2.calc.c1.g1: Chlorine: 35.5 u each, two of them
ch3.u2.calc.c1.s0: Multiply the chlorine mass by two
ch3.u2.calc.c1.trap: Adding only one chlorine. The subscript tells you how many to count.
a.ch3-u2-calc-3.title: How heavy is one atom?
a.ch3-u2-zoomscale-4.title: One atom, on the same scale
a.ch3-u2-zoomscale-4.blurb: The scale you have been climbing since the first chapter. This is the bottom of it.
ch3.u2.quiz.q0.prompt: What does the symbol Na stand for?
ch3.u2.quiz.q1.prompt: Atomic mass is measured relative to what?
ch3.u2.quiz.q1.f0: Hydrogen was used once, long ago, and then dropped.
ch3.u2.quiz.q1.o1: One sixteenth of an oxygen atom
ch3.u2.quiz.q1.f1: Oxygen was used too, and dropped, because natural oxygen is a mixture of isotopes.
ch3.u2.quiz.q1.o2: One twelfth of a carbon-12 atom
ch3.u2.quiz.q1.f2: Right. Carbon-12 has been the standard since 1961.
ch3.u2.quiz.q1.f3: A gram is far too big. One atom is nothing like a gram.
a.ch3-u2-quiz-5.title: Atoms and symbols
ch3.u3.definition: A molecule is two or more atoms held together tightly enough to behave as one unit. They can be the same element, as in oxygen gas, or different, as in water. An ion is an atom or group of atoms carrying a charge, and compounds made of ions have no molecules at all: just a lattice, repeating.
a.ch3-u3-read-1.title: Atoms rarely travel alone
ch3.u3.sort.i0.label: Argon, Ar
ch3.u3.sort.i0.why: The noble gases go about alone. They have no spare arms.
ch3.u3.sort.i1.label: Helium, He
ch3.u3.sort.i2.label: Oxygen, O2
ch3.u3.sort.i2.why: Two oxygen atoms, which is why the formula has a subscript.
ch3.u3.sort.i3.label: Hydrogen, H2
ch3.u3.sort.i4.label: Chlorine, Cl2
ch3.u3.sort.i5.label: Phosphorus, P4
ch3.u3.sort.i6.label: Sulphur, S8
ch3.u3.sort.i6.why: Eight, in a ring. The yellow powder from the last chapter.
a.ch3-u3-sort-2.title: How many atoms travel together?
a.ch3-u3-sort-2.blurb: Atomicity is just the count of atoms in one molecule of the element.
a.ch3-u3-classifytree-3.title: Atom, molecule or ion?
a.ch3-u3-classifytree-3.blurb: Three questions, and anything you meet in this chapter lands somewhere.
ch3.u3.quiz.q0.o0: An ion made of one atom with several charges
ch3.u3.quiz.q0.f0: That describes an ion with a high charge, not a polyatomic one.
ch3.u3.quiz.q0.o1: A group of atoms bonded together, carrying a charge as a group
ch3.u3.quiz.q0.f1: Right. Sulphate and ammonium are groups that move and react as one unit.
ch3.u3.quiz.q0.f2: Being in solution has nothing to do with it.
ch3.u3.quiz.q0.o3: An atom that has lost more than one electron
ch3.u3.quiz.q0.f3: Still one atom, so not polyatomic.
ch3.u3.quiz.q1.prompt: Which of these is a polyatomic ion?
ch3.u3.quiz.q1.f0: One chlorine atom, so not polyatomic.
ch3.u3.quiz.q1.f2: Right. Carbonate: one carbon and three oxygens, charged as a group.
a.ch3-u3-quiz-4.title: Polyatomic ions
ch3.u4.definition: Every atom behaves as though it has a certain number of arms to hold on with, and that number is its valency. Sodium has one, magnesium two, aluminium three. A formula is correct when every arm on every atom has found a partner, with none spare on either side. Chapter 4 explains where the arms come from.
a.ch3-u4-read-1.title: Valency: how many arms an atom has
ch3.u4.valency.predict.prompt: Magnesium has two arms, chlorine has one. How many chlorine atoms does one magnesium need?
ch3.u4.valency.predict.o3: It depends on how much you have
ch3.u4.valency.observe: Did one chlorine leave an arm spare?
ch3.u4.valency.explain: Two, because magnesium's two arms each need a partner and chlorine brings one arm each. That is MgCl2, and no amount of mixing will make MgCl.
ask.ch3-u4-valencyhands-2.cao.q: Calcium has two arms and oxygen has two. Why is it CaO and not Ca2O2?
ask.ch3-u4-valencyhands-2.cao.a:
Because Ca2O2 is the same thing written twice. One calcium's two arms are exactly matched by one oxygen's two, so the pairing is already complete at one each, and doubling both sides adds nothing.

A formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio, not a headcount of a particular lump. This is the step the crossing-over trick gets wrong: cross 2 and 2 and you write Ca2O2 and never notice. Watching the arms pair up makes it obvious, because the spare arms are what you are looking for and there are none at one each.
a.ch3-u4-valencyhands-2.title: Make the arms pair up
a.ch3-u4-valencyhands-2.blurb: Add atoms until no arm is left holding nothing. The formula writes itself as you go.
ch3.u4.sort.i0.label: Magnesium chloride, MgCl2
ch3.u4.sort.i0.why: Two arms on magnesium, one on each chlorine.
ch3.u4.sort.i1.label: Calcium oxide, CaO
ch3.u4.sort.i1.why: Two arms each, matched one to one.
ch3.u4.sort.i2.label: Aluminium chloride, AlCl3
ch3.u4.sort.i2.why: Three arms on aluminium, three chlorines.
ch3.u4.sort.i3.label: Calcium carbonate, CaCO3
ch3.u4.sort.i3.why: Calcium has two arms, carbonate carries two.
ch3.u4.sort.i4.label: Sodium chloride, NaCl2
ch3.u4.sort.i4.why: Sodium has one arm. It cannot hold two chlorines.
ch3.u4.sort.i5.label: Magnesium oxide, Mg2O2
ch3.u4.sort.i5.why: Right ratio, written twice over. MgO is the formula.
ch3.u4.sort.i6.label: Aluminium oxide, AlO
ch3.u4.sort.i6.why: Three arms against two does not pair up. Al2O3 does.
a.ch3-u4-sort-3.title: Right formula or wrong?
a.ch3-u4-sort-3.blurb: The arms have to balance. Check each one.
ch3.u4.quiz.q0.prompt: Quick lime is CaO. Which elements is it made of?
ch3.u4.quiz.q0.f0: Right. Ca for calcium, O for oxygen.
ch3.u4.quiz.q0.f1: C would be carbon, but this is Ca, which is calcium.
ch3.u4.quiz.q0.f2: The O is a second element.
ch3.u4.quiz.q0.f3: There is no separate carbon here. Ca is one symbol, not C and a.
ch3.u4.quiz.q1.prompt: Hydrogen bromide is HBr. Which elements?
ch3.u4.quiz.q1.f0: B is boron, but Br is bromine. The second letter matters.
ch3.u4.quiz.q1.f2: Br is a single symbol, not B followed by r.
ch3.u4.quiz.q1.f3: He is helium. H on its own is hydrogen.
a.ch3-u4-quiz-4.title: Name the elements inside
ch3.u5.definition: Add up the atomic masses of every atom in the formula and you have the molecular mass. For something like sodium chloride there are no molecules to speak of, only a repeating lattice of ions, so the same sum is called the formula unit mass instead. The arithmetic is identical; the name admits what is actually there.
a.ch3-u5-read-1.title: Molecular mass, and when not to call it that
ch3.u5.calc.c0.prompt: What is the molecular mass of water, H2O? Hydrogen is 1 u and oxygen is 16 u.
ch3.u5.calc.c0.trap: Writing 17 by counting one hydrogen. The subscript applies to the atom before it.
ch3.u5.calc.c1.prompt: What is the molecular mass of carbon dioxide, CO2? Carbon is 12 u and oxygen is 16 u.
ch3.u5.calc.c2.prompt: What is the formula unit mass of sodium chloride, NaCl? Sodium is 23 u and chlorine is 35.5 u.
ch3.u5.calc.c2.trap: Calling it molecular mass. Sodium chloride has no molecules, only a lattice.
a.ch3-u5-calc-2.title: Add up the masses
ch3.u5.quiz.q0.prompt: Why does sodium chloride get a formula unit mass rather than a molecular mass?
ch3.u5.quiz.q0.f0: Plenty of solids are made of molecules. Sulphur is one.
ch3.u5.quiz.q0.o1: Because it is made of ions in a lattice, with no separate molecules
ch3.u5.quiz.q0.f1: Right. There is no single NaCl unit sitting apart from the rest; the formula gives the ratio in the lattice.
ch3.u5.quiz.q0.o2: Because its mass is not a whole number
ch3.u5.quiz.q0.f2: The number has nothing to do with the name.
ch3.u5.quiz.q0.f3: Containing a metal is a hint, not the reason.
a.ch3-u5-quiz-3.title: Which name, and why
lab.flask.s.sealed: The reaction in a stoppered flask
lab.flask.s.open: The same reaction, stopper left off
lab.flask.t.mix: Tilt it and let the two solutions meet
lab.flask.r.sealed.mix: The liquids fizz. Bubbles collect in the neck and stay there.
lab.flask.tells.sealed: Nothing got out, and nothing was lost. The gas is still in the flask, and it still has mass.
lab.flask.r.open.mix: The same fizzing. This time the bubbles leave the flask.
lab.flask.tells.open: 0.44 g lighter, and that is exactly the carbon dioxide that walked out. Mass was conserved; it simply stopped being yours to weigh.
mis.mass-vanishes-with-the-gas.statement: Mass is destroyed when something burns away or fizzes off.
mis.mass-vanishes-with-the-gas.correctio: The gas still exists and still weighs something. It left the flask, which is not the same as leaving the universe. Catch it and the balance is unchanged.
mis.any-ratio-makes-the-compound.stateme: You can combine two elements in whatever proportion you like.
mis.any-ratio-makes-the-compound.correct: A compound takes one fixed ratio by mass. Give it more of one element and the excess sits there unreacted.
mis.extra-reactant-joins-in.statement: Adding more of one element makes more product.
mis.extra-reactant-joins-in.correction: Only up to the point where the other element runs out. After that the extra is a spectator.
mis.symbol-is-the-english-initial.statem: Every symbol is the first letter of the element's English name.
mis.symbol-is-the-english-initial.correc: Several come from older Latin names agreed before English became the language of chemistry: Na, K, Fe, Cu and Ag.
mis.u-is-a-weight.statement: An atomic mass in u is a weight you could put on a balance.
mis.u-is-a-weight.correction: It is a ratio, not a weight: how heavy the atom is compared with one twelfth of a carbon-12 atom.
mis.crossing-over-needs-no-tidying.state: Cross the valencies over and the formula is finished.
mis.crossing-over-needs-no-tidying.corre: Crossing over gives Ca2O2 for calcium oxide, which is the same ratio written twice. A formula is the simplest whole-number ratio.
mis.polyatomic-means-big-charge.statemen: A polyatomic ion is one carrying more than one charge.
mis.polyatomic-means-big-charge.correcti: Poly refers to the number of atoms, not the size of the charge. Sulphate is many atoms sharing one charge.
mis.every-compound-has-molecules.stateme: Every compound is built from molecules.
mis.every-compound-has-molecules.correct: Ionic compounds have none. Sodium chloride is a repeating lattice, which is why its sum is called a formula unit mass.
ch3.u5.quiz.q1.prompt: Calcium carbonate is CaCO3. Calcium is 40 u, carbon 12 u and oxygen 16 u. What is its formula unit mass?
ch3.u5.quiz.q1.f0: That counts one oxygen. The 3 applies to the oxygen before it, so there are three.
ch3.u5.quiz.q1.f1: That counts two oxygens. Read the subscript again.
ch3.u5.quiz.q1.o3: absolutely nothing, it has no formula unit mass
ch3.u5.quiz.q1.f3: It has one. What it has no claim to is a molecular mass, because there are no molecules in the lattice.
ask.ch3-u3-classifytree-3.nomolecules.q: If sodium chloride has no molecules, what does NaCl even mean?
ask.ch3-u3-classifytree-3.nomolecules.a:
It means the ratio, and nothing more. In a grain of salt there is no pair of atoms you could point at and call one unit. There is a lattice: sodium ions and chloride ions alternating in every direction, for as far as the grain goes.

NaCl says that however far you go, you will find one sodium for every chloride. The formula is a census, not a picture of a particle.
ask.ch3-u5-calc-2.chlorine.q: Why is chlorine 35.5 u? Every other mass here is a whole number.
ask.ch3-u5-calc-2.chlorine.a:
Because 35.5 is an average, and nothing actually weighs it.

Chlorine comes in two kinds, one a little heavier than the other. Roughly three atoms in four are the lighter kind and one in four the heavier, and 35.5 is what you get when you average them in that proportion. Any single chlorine atom is one or the other; the 35.5 belongs to the element, not to an atom.

Why one element should come in two weights is the question Chapter 4 opens with.
aid.s.u2.meaning: The five whose symbols you cannot guess from the English name. Every other symbol in this chapter is the first letter or two of the word you already know; these five are the ones to panic about.
aid.s.u2.P.note: The one people reach for P on, and P is phosphorus.
aid.s.u2.A.note: Argent is still the word for silver in French, and on coats of arms.
aid.s.u2.N.note: Natron, the soda the Egyptians mined, is the same word.
aid.s.u2.I.note: Ferrous and ferric survive in English, which is the thread back to Fe.
aid.s.u2.C.note: Named for Cyprus, which the Romans mined it from.
recap.s.u1.q1.ask: A candle burns down to nothing. Has mass been destroyed?
recap.s.u1.q1.answer: No. The wax left as carbon dioxide and water vapour, both of which have mass. Weigh the candle, the air that went in and the gases that came out, and the total is unchanged.
recap.s.u1.q1.listenFor: Listen for a confident yes. Something getting smaller is the most natural evidence in the world that it is going away, and the whole law is the claim that your eyes are not a balance.
recap.s.u1.q2.ask: 3 g of carbon burns completely in 8 g of oxygen. If I give it 50 g of oxygen instead, how much carbon dioxide do I get?
recap.s.u1.q2.answer: Still 11 g. The carbon takes 8 g of oxygen and no more, and 42 g of oxygen is left sitting there unused.
recap.s.u1.q2.listenFor: Listen for 53 g, which is everything added up. It is the right instinct about mass applied to the wrong question: conservation says nothing vanishes, not that everything reacts.
recap.s.u2.q1.ask: Why is the symbol for sodium Na and not S?
recap.s.u2.q1.answer: S was already taken by sulphur, and the symbols were settled from Latin names so that chemists writing in different languages would write the same thing. Sodium's Latin name is natrium.
recap.s.u2.q1.listenFor: Listen for 'because sodium has two letters'. That explains Ca for calcium, but it does not explain where an N comes from when there is no N in sodium.
recap.s.u2.q2.ask: Oxygen's atomic mass is 16 u. Sixteen of what?
recap.s.u2.q2.answer: Sixteen twelfths of a carbon-12 atom. It is a comparison, not a weight: an oxygen atom is sixteen times as heavy as one twelfth of a carbon-12 atom.
recap.s.u2.q2.listenFor: Listen for any answer in grams. A u is a ratio, and an atom weighed in grams is a number with twenty-odd zeros after the point.
recap.s.u3.q1.ask: Is oxygen gas, O2, an element or a compound?
recap.s.u3.q1.answer: An element. Both atoms are oxygen, so nothing has combined with anything else. The 2 counts atoms, it does not mix substances.
recap.s.u3.q1.listenFor: Listen for 'compound, because there are two atoms in it'. The subscript is being read as evidence of combining, when all it reports is how many atoms travel together.
recap.s.u3.q2.ask: What makes sulphate, SO4 2-, different from chloride, Cl-?
recap.s.u3.q2.answer: Sulphate is five atoms bonded together carrying one charge between them as a group. Chloride is a single atom carrying its own charge.
recap.s.u3.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'sulphate has a bigger charge'. Poly is about how many atoms, not how large the charge is.
recap.s.u4.q1.ask: Calcium has a valency of 2 and oxygen has a valency of 2. Why is calcium oxide CaO and not Ca2O2?
recap.s.u4.q1.answer: Because one calcium's two arms are already exactly matched by one oxygen's two. Ca2O2 is the same ratio written twice, and a formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio.
recap.s.u4.q1.listenFor: Listen for Ca2O2 said with confidence. It is what crossing the numbers over produces, and the student who got it that way has no way of noticing, because the trick never mentions tidying up.
recap.s.u4.q2.ask: Sodium chloride is NaCl. Why can it not be NaCl2?
recap.s.u4.q2.answer: Sodium has one arm. It can hold one chlorine and there is nothing left to hold a second with.
recap.s.u4.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'because there is only one sodium'. The count of sodiums is not the reason; the number of arms on it is.
recap.s.u5.q1.ask: What is the molecular mass of carbon dioxide, CO2? Carbon is 12 u, oxygen is 16 u.
recap.s.u5.q1.answer: 44 u. One carbon at 12, two oxygens at 16 each making 32, and 12 plus 32 is 44.
recap.s.u5.q1.listenFor: Listen for 28, which is 12 plus one oxygen. The subscript was read and then not used.
recap.s.u5.q2.ask: Why do we say formula unit mass for sodium chloride rather than molecular mass?
recap.s.u5.q2.answer: Because there are no molecules in it. Sodium chloride is a lattice of ions, so there is no single NaCl unit standing apart from the rest. The sum is identical; the name admits what is actually there.
recap.s.u5.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'because it is a solid'. Sulphur is a solid made of S8 molecules, so being solid is not what decides it.

gloss.atom: The smallest piece of an element that still behaves like that element. It cannot be broken down further by any chemical reaction.
gloss.molecule: Two or more atoms held together tightly enough to move and react as one unit. They may be the same element or different ones.
gloss.ion: An atom, or a group of atoms, carrying an electric charge.
gloss.polyatomic-ion: A group of atoms bonded together that carries a charge as a group, such as sulphate or ammonium. Poly counts the atoms, not the charge.
gloss.valency: The number of arms an atom has for holding on to others. Sodium has one, magnesium two, aluminium three. A formula is right when no arm is left unpaired.
gloss.atomicity: How many atoms there are in one molecule of an element. Argon is one, oxygen two, phosphorus four, sulphur eight.
gloss.atomic-mass-unit: The scale atoms are weighed on, written u. One u is one twelfth of a carbon-12 atom, so a mass in u is a comparison rather than a weight.
gloss.molecular-mass: The atomic masses of every atom in a molecule, added up.
gloss.formula-unit-mass: The same sum as a molecular mass, used for substances that have no molecules. Sodium chloride is a lattice of ions, so its formula gives a ratio rather than a particle.
gloss.lattice: A repeating arrangement of ions extending in every direction, with no separate molecules anywhere in it.
gloss.chemical-formula: The symbols and numbers that say which elements a compound contains and in what simplest whole-number ratio.
gloss.element: A substance made of only one kind of atom. Oxygen gas is still an element: both atoms in O2 are oxygen.
gloss.compound: A substance made of two or more elements chemically joined in a fixed ratio by mass.
gloss.conservation-of-mass: Mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. It is why an equation has to balance.
gloss.constant-proportions: A compound always contains the same elements in the same ratio by mass, however it was made.
